[Editor's note: The statement is as follows:]
Statement by the Dominion Council of Health
on Live Oral Poliovirus Vaccine (Sabin)
The dominion council of health believes that live poliovirus Sabin vaccine offers a great potential for the control of paralytic poliomyelitis in Canada. In September the national technical advisory committee on live poliovirus vaccines, under the chairmanship of Dr. A. J. Rhodes, director, school of hygiene, University of Toronto, recommended that immunization programs using the live oral Sabin vaccine be temporarily deferred. The reason for this recommendation was to permit a full investigation of all cases of poliomyelitis and other acute diseases of the nervous system, which simulate poliomyelitis, and which occurred in Canada this year. This was to determine what association there might be between these cases and live poliovirus vaccine.
Since September 13 a full investigation has been carried out across Canada concerning poliomyelitis and polio-like diseases, with intensive study of those cases which might in any way be associated with Sabin vaccine. Many persons, family physicians, medical specialists, medical officers of health, local poliomyelitis committees, virologists and epidemiologists assisted in this investigation. Committee members were personally engaged in the assessment of cases in their own provinces. Members of the committee visited Europe and Japan to obtain first hand information concerning the extensive use of live oral poliovirus vaccine in those areas. Direct reports were received from New Zealand, Great Britain and the United States. The technical advisory committee met on November 5 and 6 to consider all the available evidence and it received first hand

Statement on Use of Sabin Vaccine accounts of experience in the United States from a representative of the United States public health service.
The committee reviewed detailed information concerning all known polio-like illness in Canada this year that might in any way be associated with live poliovirus vaccine. There were no deaths in these cases. In the approximately four million persons fed Sabin vaccine in May, June, and July, there were four cases of paralytic disease with a high probability of association with Sabin vaccine. These are the same four cases mentioned in Mr. Monteith's September 13 statement. Among contacts to those fed Sabin vaccine earlier this year, one case of paralytic poliomyelitis was considered by the committee to have a high probability of association with Sabin vaccine. The predominant virus in these cases was Sabin vaccine virus type III. Of the remaining 26 cases of polio-like illness studied in detail, and considered by the committee as justifying close appraisal, 10 were considered to have no association with Sabin vaccine and the others were believed to have a moderate or slight probability of association.
Experience with live oral Sabin vaccine in other countries has had a spectacular effect in reducing the incidence of paralytic poliomyelitis.
After a careful review of all the evidence the expert committee recommended the following procedures, for the present, for immunization against poliomyelitis in Canada:
1.	That Salk vaccine, in combination with other antigens, or alone, remain, for the present, the basic vaccine for protection against poliomyelitis for all age groups. Particular emphasis should be placed on the Salk vaccination of children under one year of age.
2.	That trivalent oral poliovirus vaccine be incorporated in routine immunization programs to follow an initial course of Salk vaccine to further diminish the circulation of wild polio viruses.
3.	That, in areas with a risk of poliomyelitis, any form of Sabin poliovirus vaccine be used on a community-wide basis.
4.	That Sabin vaccine, types I and II, could be used freely for all age groups.
5.	That, in all circumstances, when oral poliovirus vaccine is used, it be on a carefully planned and supervised basis. The following are considered essential components of such programs:
(i)	Planning and supervision should be conducted by departments of health.

(ii)	Immunization programs with live poliovirus vaccine should be directed primarily to children. Children are the main reservoir of infection in Canada and in restricting the circulation of wild polio viruses in this group, a degree of protection will thereby be afforded to adults.
(iii)	Active surveillance and prompt reporting of all cases of nervous system disease occurring within 60 days of vaccine feedings should be required.
(iv)	Contraindications to the use of Sabin vaccine are:
(a)	Acute febrile illness
(b)	Debilitating disease
(c)	Administration within 21 days of another live virus vaccine, e.g., smallpox and yellow fever vaccines.
6.	That there be prompt and direct exchange of information with other countries concerning the safety and efficacy of oral poliovirus vaccine.
The dominion council of health recommends that the use of Sabin vaccine be deferred no longer and endorses these recommendations as to its use. Specific plans will be determined by provincial departments of health.

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF MODIFICATION OF IMPORT SURCHARGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a statement to make with respect to the further relaxation of surcharges. In view of the continued improvement in the foreign exchange reserves, the government has decided that it is now possible to take a second significant step in relaxing the import surcharges. The first step was announced on October 16; it covered some $250 million worth of industrial machinery and equipment of a class or kind not made in Canada, and certain other items.
This second relaxation is designed to be of direct assistance to every Canadian consumer and to keep down the cost of living. To this end the surcharges on practically all foods and agricultural and fisheries products are being removed. In taking this step we have had in mind that we are entering that period of the year in which our requirements for imported foods are particularly marked. When the surcharges were first applied, many food items-oranges, bananas, orange juice, tea and coffee-were exempted. With this present relaxation only a short list of luxury or less essential products, such as pate de foie gras, truffles and brandied fruits, and

one or two other items such as that will remain subject to the surcharge. Wines and spirits, tobacco and tobacco products and confectionery remain subject to the surcharge.
The following are examples of the goods being freed from surcharge: raisins and dried fruits, biscuits, fancy molasses, fresh and canned meats, cattle, poultry, peanut butter, yeast, milk foods, prepared cereal foods, pearl barley, peas and beans, corn meal, macaroni, canned fruits and vegetables, fresh and frozen vegetables, olives, kippered herring and sardines. The surcharge is also being reduced or eliminated on certain other products. Printing machinery and equipment covered by tariff items 412b and 412d, by and large, are not available from Canadian sources; the removal of the surcharge should be of assistance to the printing and publishing industry. The surcharge is being removed from ambulances.
Two major consumer items, refrigerators and carpets, have carried a surcharge of 15 per cent, the rate applied to less essential goods. It now seems appropriate to reduce to 10 per cent the surcharge on these products and thus to bring them into line with other major household goods used by Canadian consumers.
This second relaxation covers about $220 million of foods and agricultural and fisheries products, in terms of the annual rate of imports, and about $40 million of other goods, to a total of $260 million. It is further concrete evidence of the government's intention to remove the surcharges as soon as circumstances permit. It should be of real assistance to every Canadian consumer, and will ease the burden of the surcharges on our trading partners who have an interest in selling us these various products.
These removals and reductions in surcharge will take effect as from tomorrow.

HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
1.	Has the Department of National Health and Welfare investigated the circumstances of the case of smallpox entering Canada a short time ago and, if so, what were they?
2.	Has the department reviewed the regulations with the object of ascertaining whether these may be made safer for Canadians?

subtopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
1. Yes. A fourteen year old boy came from Laranjeiras do Sul, Parana State, Brazil, where an outbreak of smallpox (alastrim or variola minor) existed, being regarded by local authorities as chicken pox. Before departure for Canada and without vaccination having been performed a certificate of vaccination was issued by the local medical officer on the form of the local health department and bearing the medical officer's signature and the official stamp of the secretariat of public health of the local area.
The boy entered the United States-Canada quarantine pool area at New York, reaching Toronto by train on August 12. The next day he developed the prodromal rash of smallpox (variola minor or alastrim) which was diagnosed clinically on August 17 and confirmed by laboratory tests August 20. The patient was isolated first at home and later in River-dale isolation hospital where he made an uneventful recovery.
Family contacts and all other persons who were known to be contacts were kept under surveillance and vaccination was offered to persons who could have been exposed. Many other persons in the Toronto area also took advantage of this opportunity and underwent vaccination or revaccination for their personal protection. Fortunately there were no secondary cases.
2.	Extensive international travel makes the introduction of smallpox an ever present possibility. Quarantine measures are designed not as an absolute guarantee against the importation of smallpox but to reduce the hazard of
Questions
importing the disease by employing measures of practical value but which do not seriously interfere with international traffic. The international sanitary regulations are taken as a guide to what is practical and reasonable. These as well as the Canadian quarantine regulations are continually under review.

2.	It is not known what level of strontium 90 in milk constitutes a danger to humans. The possible danger from any particular level depends on how long the level is maintained. The recommendations of the international commission on radiological protection can be interpreted to suggest that, for levels which are maintained for an indefinitely long period, a level of 79 micromicrocuries per gram of dietary calcium is permissible for Canada. It should be emphasized however that this is not a danger level, but rather one for which there is very little probability of observing ill effects in Canadians.

4.	It is not known what level of iodine 131 constitutes a danger to humans. No ill effects have yet been observed in children who have received medical doses of 5-10 microcuries of iodine 131 during the past five or six years. In terms of maximum permissible concentrations of iodine 131 in milk resulting from radioactive fall-out, a guide level similar to that for strontium 90 has not been set because of the short half life of iodine 131 and the dependency of iodine 131 levels on the pattern of nuclear testing and subsequent meteorological and climatological conditions. The recommendations of the international commission on radiological protection can be interpreted to suggest that, for levels which are maintained for an indefinitely long period, a level of about 3,000 micromicrocuries per gram of dietary potassium is permissible for Canada. subtopic: FOOD AND DRUG DIRECTORATE
FOOD AND DRUG DIRECTORATE
speechtext:
1.	How many persons in the food and drug directorate review the new drug submissions, and what are the qualifications of these persons?
2.	Does the food and drug directorate confirm animal toxicity reports done by the drug manufacturer and, if so, how often?
3.	Does the food and drug directorate require tests for teratogenicity on all new drugs?
4.	Do drug manufacturers, drug importers, and drug distributors, require a licence to operate in Canada and, if not, what is the reason?
5.	Does the food and drug directorate have a standard for laboratory technique which all drug manufacturers must follow in the preparation and testing of drugs?

subtopic: FOOD AND DRUG DIRECTORATE
speechtext:
1. New drug submissions are assigned for review to members of the professional staff of the food and drug directorate who have expert knowledge of the type of drug dealt with in the submission. These reviews are carried out as part of their duties and the time required is equivalent to approximately four persons working full time.
The staff performing these reviews as part time duties are graduates in medicine and science with postgraduate degrees and training in biochemistry, bacteriology, chemistry, pharmacy, physiology and pharmacology.
2.	No confirmation of the animal toxicity reports of the drug manufacturer is done unless there is reason to doubt such reports. This does not occur very often.
3.	No recognized animal tests have been developed for detecting the teratogenic effects of drugs in humans. Where a drug is recommended for continuous administration and may be used by a wide segment of the population, it has been the practice to require drug manufacturers to subject such drugs to chronic toxicity tests in laboratory animals. This involves administering the drug for one or two

Questions
years and over two or three generations of the animals, noting any malformations of the offspring and any other side effects of the drug.
4.	It is beyond the authority of the Food and Drugs Act to licence an industry. However provision has been made in sections 12 and 37 of the act to prohibit the sale of certain drug products such as serums, toxins, vaccines, parenteral antibiotics, insulin, amphetamines, barbiturates, etc., unless certain defined requirements have been met. speechtext: Is the minister going to make a statement?

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, usually in introducing the estimates of the Department of Agriculture the minister reviews the highlights of the expenditures and sometimes he takes some aspect of agriculture and gives a particular review of it. Last Monday an attempt was made to adjourn the business of the house in order to discuss my speech to the Saskatchewan wheat pool. Therefore that makes it very clear and necessary for me to open my remarks by discussing that speech and some of the remarks made about it by other people.
Needless to say, I was surprised at the leader of the New Democratic party taking the position he did in regard to the operation of the Canadian wheat board. To say the least, he could not be more wrong in his understanding of how the wheat board operates. However, I shall refer to that part of the subject later in my remarks.
In putting forward to the Saskatchewan wheat pool two propositions for consideration and discussion by western Canadian farmers during the next few months, I was doing what I have always done and what I promised the farmers I would do, namely, to discuss with them first all matters affecting them personally before bringing such matters forward for government consideration.
Mr. Chairman, anyone who has observed my methods of operation during the last few years will fully recognize that I have used this technique of consultation over and over again, and I would suggest that the course I have followed in stimulating discussion has been warmly welcomed by farmers. It has brought about a spirit of co-operation between the minister and the farmers and their organizations which has not existed for a good many years.
[Mr. Matheson.l
As an example of this type of technique I would point out that one of the first moves I made on becoming Minister of Agriculture was to speak in many parts of the country outlining the government's long range national development and national agricultural program. After doing that I would raise questions with the farmers about things we thought should be discussed, such as the problems of farmers in marginal areas and on marginal land, and would raise queries about such matters as the low income of certain sections of the farm economy.
To stimulate discussion I put forward suggestions myself and I asked for other ideas. Hon. members will remember I was called many things such as "the pothole farmer," and "the Christmas tree minister." Such names and epithets were hurled at me because I used the technique of discussing with farmers the problems that existed, and asked for their advice on how the problems should be met. As I say, I did this in order to get their reactions, so that then I might come before my colleagues with something I knew had been tried and tested in the minds of the people who were going to be affected by it.
As a result of such direct discussions with farmers, farm organizations and government leaders at other levels, we were able to introduce a rehabilitation and development act which is now receiving the enthusiastic co-operation of ten provincial governments together with the co-operation of farm organizations and thousands of farmers and ordinary Canadians all across the dominion. As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, even though the ten master agreements have been signed, and even though between 75 and 100 project agreements are now before the federal government for consideration, I am still discussing ARDA with those I feel can offer something tangible for its improvement.
As late as last Monday, when the discussion to which I have referred arose in the house, I spent two hours with the farm writers of Canada discussing ARDA. I put forward suggestions at the meeting with them, 1 received suggestions in return and all I can say is that the policy is working.
Another example of the same sort of technique stems from the introduction by the previous minister of agriculture of the Farm Credit Act. He promised the house that as soon as sufficient experience was gained and if there were any ideas forthcoming that would improve the legislation, they would be brought before the house. In fact at this very moment we have as an item of business amendments to the Farm Credit Act.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CRITICISM OF CANADIAN
speechtext: I moved them.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CRITICISM OF CANADIAN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall come to the hon. gentleman later. I have discussed farm credit with farmers who have received it and with farmers who have not. I have discussed it with government officials and bank officials. I have raised it in public discussions pointing out what I thought were ideas to improve it, and I got the farmers' reactions to those ideas. As a result of all that we are now introducing amendments to the act which will not only make it more flexible but will make it, as it was described by the New Democratic party, most revolutionary legislation. One does not get that kind of comment from the N.D.P. unless it is really something they have not thought of.
What is the contribution of the hon. member for Assiniboia to this debate? Day after day he tells us that this amending bill does not do justice to the small farmer. In reply I would say to him, let him read what the agricultural commentators are saying about his position and what he is doing. Not only does the bill help small farmers in its present form but it will help them even more as a result of the consultations I have had with farmers across the country. He has the nerve to stand up in this august chamber and talk about horses. He says horses are not mentioned in this act. He is trying to follow in the footsteps of a previous member from Saskatchewan who was minister of agriculture at a time when farmers could not sell their grain because they were producing too much of it, and the then minister urged them to turn their grain fields back into pastures to feed horses. This is the horsepower member over there now. He has mentioned that he introduced amendments into this act. These amendments were nonsensical.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CRITICISM OF CANADIAN
speechtext: So nonsensical that you accepted them.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CRITICISM OF CANADIAN
speechtext:
In effect, all he wants to do is to be able to stand up and say he introduced amendments and the minister accepted them. I am only trying to do one thing, Mr. Chairman. I am trying to get good legislation on the statute books and constantly keep amending it. If it gives the hon. member any small, tactical victory to be able to go to the farmers and say he added something to the act, then as long as that amendment does not hurt the act I will accept it. I just want to get the act amended for those 2,000 or 3,000 farmers who want to benefit from it this winter. I feel, Mr. Chairman, that the democratic process demands that there be discussion with citizens of the nation as well as discussion with hon. members in this house before legislation is passed.
The leader of the New Democratic party states, according to Hansard, that before
Supply-Agriculture
constituents discuss these two proposals, members of parliament should have the opportunity to discuss their implication. Such a doctrine would mean that the minister would have to seek approval of any suggestion he might wish to make to the government, farm organizations and so on, before he actually made it. The nonsensical nature of this approach is self-evident. However, I welcome the opportunity of repeating my remarks to the Saskatchewan wheat pool in the House of Commons. I am going to quote from the remarks that I made to the wheat pool last Friday. In opening my remarks I said:
There are two main subjects I would like to put on record today and I intend to introduce them in a manner which will provoke discussion.
Little did I realize how far that discussion would go.
Traditionally, what we say here is reserved for this room, but as far as I am concerned my remarks can be used publicly. The reasons for this are: first, part of my speech is for information purposes and I would like to reach as many people as possible, and-
I certainly did, thanks to some hon. members.
-second, I want to put forward a series of proposals which are in my mind in the hope that there will be public discussion during the winter of these matters.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I would say the thesis of these remarks was simply that there was a great opportunity to sell even more of our wheat now if everybody pulls together; that was the thesis of the remarks I made. First, I pointed out in the tables which were attached to the speech the great use of credit and government assisted sales by the United States and Canada. In my remarks, I made known the tremendous credit sales made by Australia, Canada, France and the United States in the last few months. From this information I drew the conclusion that Canada's surplus position would not be the low position it is today if it had not been for this government's move into credit sales. I gave the relative figures. At the present time, under the Export Credits Insurance Act some $90 million is committed to insure wheat sales to Poland and Czechoslovakia. In addition, there were special government guarantees involving a credit of $100 million to mainland China.
I went on to point out that the government was planning to increase credit sales. I mentioned that the very first bill introduced in this very important session, when international payments are so much in our minds, was a bill to double the fund under section 21 of the Export Credits Insurance Act from $200 million to $400 million. In my speech, I outlined what the government did to get the world food program under FAO and

Supply-Agriculture
the United Nations into operation. Then, I elaborated as follows:-I wish hon. members would follow this closely because this is the basis of my later proposition-
Although food disposal under the auspices of either a multilateral world food program or bilateral action is good in itself, I believe that the potential in commercial fields is even more important. There are approximately two billion people in the newly developing countries of the world. Their main industry, at the moment, is agriculture. They usually produce one or more staple product and these products have a market characteristic similar to wheat prior to the acceptance of the first international wheat agreement. That is, prices and returns to producers tended to fluctuate widely and, as we well know in the prairies, these fluctuations caused most serious harm to farm Income and stability.
The Canadian government, through its membership in several international organizations, over the past year has been launching large-scale efforts to persuade the industrial nations of western Europe, which usually have food surpluses, to take the lead in setting up international commodity agreements, product by product. Some of these products are temperate foods that we produce and others are products from the warmer areas of the world in which most of the newly developing nations are found.
It is my thought that if we could give to these newly developing nations stabilized floor prices- through international commodity agreements-for their staple products, we could raise their standard of living to a marked degree. If we assumed that such a group of commodity agreements could increase the standard of living for these people by only one dollar per person annually, the tremendous potential market that would then become available is apparent. Certainly, for many years to come, a good proportion of that extra income would be spent on food. That is why I think there is some weight in my argument that the commercial potential for the sale of temperate foods in these newly developing countries far outweighs the reasonable expectations of a growth in world programs for free distribution of foods. Oddly enough, this type of approach makes the farmers at both ends of the trading arrangement happier.
This, Mr. Chairman, demonstrates how I was trying to develop the theme of increased new sales in new areas. I went on to state in the speech how the Canadian wheat board has set up a technical service for our customers and how the Canadian flour milling companies were co-operating by setting up mills in countries where we thought there could be an expansion for the consumption of bread. I emphasized the aggressive acts of this government now and in the future to increase sales.
Next I spoke of the very high levies which we have to overcome to get into the E.E.C. markets. Having demonstrated the increased competitiveness of the present world wheat markets, I asked their assistance in examining new techniques to increase sales. To that end I put forward two suggestions for their consideration during the months ahead. These suggestions may be accepted or rejected, but at least I feel that the farmers have a right to participate in discussions on these points

so that they will have some say in what they want to do. This technique that I have followed may be new to some here, but it is not new to the farmers.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CRITICISM OF CANADIAN
speechtext: It is new to the Prime Minister.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CRITICISM OF CANADIAN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have in my hand the 1959 resolutions of the Saskatchewan wheat pool. Read these resolutions that were passed and you will find suggestions like this for sales promotion:
We recommend to the government of Canada that a levy of one tenth of a cent per bushel be deducted from an interim or the final payment on wheat to provide a fund, controlled by the producer, to be used in the promotion of increased utilization and sale of wheat and wheat products.
There is hardly a month passes that I do not have discussions with dairy producers, cheese producers and other producers and their organizations in general. The reason for this is simply that the great majority of farmers desire to help themselves and be independent. This has been forgotten by many politicians. Certainly I would think that today in western Canada many farmers are conscious of the fact that the higher prices they are now receiving did not all come from the devaluation of the dollar, but from the increased sales of our wheat which reduced our supplies, making it possible to have higher prices. They are aware of the significance of the Leader of the Opposition going as far away as he could from the western farmers, way down to Halifax, and making certain criticisms down there of the sales of wheat to communist China. They are very much aware of this.
I suggest, too, that the farmers of eastern Canada have become very much aware of his community of interest with the western farmers in maintaining their exports, because they know that when the western farmers export surplus grain it brings new opportunities to eastern farmers in hogs and cattle. I know that is so, both in price and in quantity sold. I mentioned earlier, Mr. Chairman, that there is a difference between sales under the Export Credits Insurance Act and the special guarantee we have for China. This government has used the Export Credits Insurance Act more widely than ever before. It is clear that we intend to use it even more. That is why we doubled the amount under section 21. But it is an insurance act. There has to be some form of established credit rating before you can make loans under this act. Under this act, for instance, a businessman pays a premium which protects him for 85 per cent of his losses; the other 15 per cent he bears himself, if there is any loss. I think that businessmen are learning to use this act and are going to use it a great deal more.

Now I ask the committee to look at what the leader of the New Democratic party said.
I am quoting now from the Winnipeg Free Press of Monday, November 12. I do not think I need warn anybody from the west to be careful about the Winnipeg Free Press. It is the last stand of the nineteenth century Gladstonian Liberal. No one has succeeded yet in dragging them screaming into this century. But they certainly dragged somebody else screaming into this century. Listen to this. This is what the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam said:
He said that the suggestion that the prairie farmers should share a portion of losses on credit sales raised the question as to why a figure of $190 million should constitute a ceiling. At the present time the government accepts liabilities of up to $400 million under the Export Credits Insurance Act on commodities and products other than wheat, he pointed out.
It is sort of startling, I know. They went on to say:
"It is, therefore, difficult to understand why Mr. Hamilton should require participation by prairie wheat growers in order to persuade his colleagues to underwrite additional credit for the sale of wheat", said Mr. Douglas.
Mr. Chairman, we make no bones about it; we intend to give more credit for wheat or any other product. This was demonstrated by the introduction of the bill by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. New countries are entering the commercial markets, countries which have no credit rating at the beginning of their trading relations with the rest of us. We would like to do something for them, and special ratings have to be made. It is evident from the remarks I quoted from my speech in Regina that I believe there is a tremendous potential for new markets, that do not even exist today, in some of these newly developing nations. I use as an example Japan, where we have seen a change from a rice economy to one of a partial wheat economy, or at least a bread economy. Japan buys for cash, it is true, but there will be many countries which may be interested in using bread as a food and which will require some form of short range or medium type credit.
I cannot speak for the government ahead of these cases arising, as each case will have to be dealt with on its merits. The government is responsible to the people for the risks they take in any credit guarantees of a special nature, and it seemed to me that western farmers should be given the opportunity to consider that they, like businessmen, might be willing, in their own interests to share with the government in some of these operations outside the Export Credits Insurance Act entirely, because the Export Credits Insurance Act, as I said before, is an insurance

act. Wheat now takes up most of the money available, and as far as I am concerned, I hope it keeps on doing that. If the farmers decide that they want to do this, they will benefit, the taxpayer will certainly benefit and the governments will want to play their full part.
I have no illusions that if accepted by farmers this is a development which will take place quickly, or that we will have a need for it immediately; but I can see the day, five or ten years from now, when such a credit fund built up in the meantime might make it easier for governments to make decisions.

I want to thank hon. members for their solicitude in wishing to hear more of my remarks. I think this indicates

they have had some effect on the committee. I can only promise hon. members that the best is yet to come.
I intend to read, now, the paragraph on page 7 of this pamphlet under the heading "Wheat Board Agents".
In carrying out its task of merchandising wheat, oats and barley produced in western Canada, the board endeavours to make full use of all agencies and services which it considers can usefully contribute to sales. The actual merchandising, particularly in the case of wheat, is a combined and complex operation involving the board and its overseas offices, the entire Canadian grain trade in all its various functions, the railways and lake steamship companies, the trade commissioner service and, in some instances, the government of Canada.
Subject to certain standards and to having the necessary facilities, financial and otherwise, to offer wheat for sale in world markets, the board enters into agreements with the shipping and exporting segments of the Canadian grain trade under which they undertake to act as agents of the board for that purpose.
The value of the shippers and exporters in this connection is due to their knowledge of the domestic and export trade in grain and especially to the fact that the firms concerned are represented, either by direct office or otherwise, in practically every country in the world which imports grain. This branch of the grain trade represents a highly developed form of enterprise, alert and keenly competitive. The success in business of the companies engaged in export depends upon their ability to sell grain in overseas markets in competition with others, and this requires considerable skill, knowledge and experience. The board has considered their services most valuable in offering wheat for sale abroad.
I read that to make it clear what the position of the board is. For the most part, the Canadian wheat board does not sell grain. It markets the grain through its agents; it turns the grain over to agents to sell.
At this time I should like to pay my regards to the tremendously efficient work of the agents of the Canadian wheat board over the years. In this highly competitive business they have done a good job. Canada's share of the cash markets of the world is increasing, and these companies handle almost all of this business. However, even though they have done a good job, I, as the minister responsible to parliament and to the people for the sale of Canadian wheat must naturally urge them to put even more drive into their efforts. I am doing that.
I said that generally speaking the Canadian wheat board does not sell wheat. Certainly, under the attitude that existed when the Liberals were in power-we all remember the statement "If the people want to buy our wheat let them come and get it"-the wheat board did not sell as much as it could have done, had there been proper encouragement from the government. Once again, let me read from this pamphlet. I am quoting now from

page 8 under the heading "Direct Govern-ment-to-Government Sales of Wheat":
In cases when a foreign government or an agency of a foreign government prefers to deal direct with the board in the matter of the purchase of grain, the board arranges to do so. On the other hand, it will not enter into direct competition with its own agents in sales to other importers, but it does encourage competition between its agents. To enter into competition with its agents would be most unethical, as the agents do not receive a commission on sales from the board but must rely on what they can earn by obtaining a sales price in excess of what they pay to purchase the wheat from the board, which is the board's asking price at time of purchase.
In recent years, with the freeing from wartime government restriction of much of the grain trade throughout the world, the actual portion of sales made directly by board agents has continued to increase in relation to total sales. However, it may be of interest to know that in the past the board has had master sales agreements with a number of countries-
A long list of countries is then given. I repeat:
The actual portion of sales made directly by board agents has continued to increase in relation to total sales.
I might point out that this refers particularly to cash sales. To continue the quotation:
Even when a sale is made directly by the board, the agents still play an important role in its fulfilment as in most cases supplementary contracts, subject to the master sales agreements referred to above, are entered into between them and the buyer concerned.

He has laid down the doctrine that it is important for him, as the Minister of Agriculture, to have discussions on agricultural policy outside the house before he has them not only inside the house but with the cabinet and his own government. The minister does not always carry out that particular technique. There are times of course, when he has discussions outside the house on cabinet policy on devaluation after that policy decision has been taken. There have also been other indications of additional changing techniques of government discussion. We have had recently, discussion on defence policy outside the house by a high official of the Conservative party, which may or may not have been inspired in Ottawa, but which certainly laid down what was meant to be the policy of the party in question.
Among some other aspects of agricultural policy the minister discussed what ARDA is doing. It cannot do very much without the co-operation of the provinces. He also discussed what the wheat board is doing. But there is no division of view on this side of the house on that. He spent most of his time however on his Regina speech, and I can understand why he did that. If I have taken him down correctly, he said among other things: "Little did I realize when I made my speech in Regina how far the discussion would go". Well, it has gone far, Mr. Chairman, right into the Prime Minister's office, according to reports, and it has gone into this debate. Perhaps that is a very good idea, in view of the strange doctrine that the minister is now putting forward, and in view of some of the proposals which he made in his Regina speech.
Among other things the minister made quite a plea for international commodity agreements. I am sure there is no division of opinion in this committee on the desirability of that. Perhaps one of the things which might happen as a result of the entry of the United Kingdom into the common market if that does take place, will be an increased effort on the part of western European countries, in which I hope the United States and Canada will participate, to bring about world commodity agreements, which the common market countries have been talking about as one way to solve our international agricultural problems. Incidentally, perhaps the only successful international commodity agreement of recent months has been one which was negotiated in New York not long ago under the auspices of the United Nations to cover international trade in coffee. All hon. members will be delighted to know that the

Supply-Agriculture
chairman of that conference, and the man so largely responsible for its success, was the Liberal candidate for Eglinton during the recent election.
Mr. Chairman, the minister has told us that his new technique, or his old technique newly applied in Regina, was to discuss matters with farmers and agricultural people outside the house; and then, as a result of that discussion and the proposals which were made in that discussion, and only then, to take these matters up with his colleagues in the cabinet as Minister of Agriculture. Indeed, at one moment in his statement he said: "I cannot speak for the government in these matters". If the Minister of Agriculture cannot speak for the government in these matters, Mr. Chairman, who can speak for the government?

I do not mind my hon. friend interrupting. I have unlimited time, so it is all right with me. The Prime Minister, when this matter was brought to his attention in the house the other day by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, first of all, had this to say, as reported at page 1510 of Hansard:
-the text of the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture . .. made perfectly clear that the expression of these views-
And they were certainly important views-
-in no way represents government policy.
In other words, this was a personal visit only on the part of the minister, who was speaking in his personal capacity to his audience in Regina. He spoke as an individual. Well, the text does not bear out either the Prime Minister's statement or indeed the minister's confirmation of that statement this afternoon; and he has, of course, no alternative but to confirm that statement.
I say that, because the minister's first words to the Saskatchewan wheat pool at their annual meeting on November 9 were these: "Mr. Chairman, this is my second official visit to the Saskatchewan wheat pool. The first was two years ago". In other words, as Minister of Agriculture he was paying an official visit to the meeting of the Saskatchewan wheat pool. Now presumably we are asked to believe that anything which he said to his audience at his official visit was purely personal and individual and that he did not speak for the government at all.
' Well, Mr. Chairman, that is ridiculous and a complete denial of cabinet responsibility, cabinet solidarity, cabinet collectivity, and indeed responsible parliamentary government; to say that the Minister of Agriculture can

make an official visit to the Saskatchewan wheat pool and put forward proposals in his personal, individual capacity, about which presumably the cabinet knew nothing at all. Are we really to believe, notwithstanding what the minister has said, that these proposals-I will be having something to say about them, because they are important-were put forward in his personal capacity, and then, having done that, that he asked for their consideration and discussion by all those concerned, treating them merely as personal suggestions on his part? If this is true, Mr. Chairman, then he was certainly perpetrating a hoax on his listeners, because it is perfectly clear to those who listened to him and to those who read his speech that this subsequent laboured explanation, was made in order to get out of an embarrassing position; it is intended to show that he was speaking only personally on this official visit, that he was taking no official responsibility at all, let alone speaking for the government as a minister.
It seems to me that even the Prime Minister himself had some second thoughts about this, because on page 1511 of Hansard for last Friday he was asked by the hon. member for Assiniboia:
Were these tentative suggestions-
As they were called-
-discussed with the government before the Minister of Agriculture put them forward in Regina?
What was the Prime Minister's reply? "Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman, of course, has no appreciation of cabinet solidarity and responsibility or he would not be asking that question." In other words, of course, these matters were discussed in the cabinet before the minister went to Saskatchewan because otherwise the hon. gentleman would not have any understanding of cabinet solidarity or cabinet responsibility in asking such a question. The fact is that it was only subsequently that this laboured explanation of the minister's personal responsibility for the statement was made in the light of what these statements were. Indeed the minister himself indicated that on this occasion as on other occasions he was not averse to saying something about his colleagues and on lifting again the veil of cabinet responsibility and cabinet secrecy, when he said this, according to his own statement on page 6, which would indicate that this was certainly a matter which had been considered by the cabinet. Talking about credit sales and their importance and the desirability of negotiating them, and we will come to that matter later, he cited the $190 million credit position for sales, the current contingent liability for China of

$100 million and $90 million for Czechoslovakia and Poland. Then he added this and I am quoting from his statement:
It was not an easy or simple matter to attain approval for these credit levels-
Presumably from his cabinet colleagues.
-and I must advise you that it will become infinitely more difficult to obtain approval for higher levels,-
Hence the Prime Minister's preoccupation with this matter is not only preoccupation with the agricultural producers. It is obviously preoccupation with his cabinet colleagues. It all goes to show, of course, that he was speaking as Minister of Agriculture. It was in that capacity that he was invited to speak. Either he spoke as Minister of Agriculture at this meeting or he had no right to speak at all in the way in which he spoke. Naturally everyone who heard him or who read his speech assumed that he was expressing the views, policies and ideas of the government of which he was a member. If the minister's proposals, suggestions and ideas are to be repudiated by the Prime Minister and the government, then indeed that puts him in a very difficult position. If they are not to be repudiated, then presumably the government accepts the responsibility for the minister's statement as that is the only way in which cabinet solidarity and cabinet responsibility can be understood.

I can, of course, understand the government's desire to crawl from under this most recent indiscretion of the minister or this new gaff, if I may call it that, of the exuberantly agreeable Minister of Agriculture. In his statement he took a good deal of credit, as he has done previously, for credit sales of wheat and other grains. There is no difference, of course, on this side of the chamber, as to the desirability in conditions today and indeed in conditions as they have existed for a good many years, of selling as much wheat as possible under credit when we cannot make those sales for cash. Indeed, in a table attached to the minister's own speech, and with which he is no doubt familiar, he showed that in 1952-53 and in 1955-56 credit sales reached proportions which were much higher than they were when this government took over until, I think the year before last when they were about equal to the year 1955-56. Then I know they went up last year largely because of credit sales to communist China.
I recall, Mr. Chairman, years ago a Liberal government beginning this process of selling wheat for credit and that when we made credit arrangements in those years with Poland, Czechoslovakia and with the Soviet union, and I had something to do with that negotiation, the criticism of the Tory opposition at that time was both sharp and shrill. They objected to this kind of thing.
I am glad that the present sales are being made now. I think it is inevitable and essential in the days in which we live that we use our bargaining powers through credits to compete with the increasing competition we get from other wheat exporters. But let it be remembered, Mr. Chairman, that while we engage in credit sales, if we do so at the expense of our cash sales, we lose. The proportion of cash sales to credit sales in the years I have mentioned under a Liberal regime was a good deal higher than it was

last year under a Conservative regime. Let it be remembered also, Mr. Chairman, that when we make credit sales we should be extremely careful to know what we are doing and to be sure that the terms we give are right and that the credit terms we give are those that do not discriminate against our friends and are those that will be met by those to whom we give them. When we made these credit deals under contract, and according to the minister there is no "contract" now with communist China; according to the minister we must not even talk about communist China; in any event, an agreement was made with the communist government in Peking and when that agreement was made we were not given all the details of the agreement. We were not given even the date on which the agreement was signed, and for a very good reason. However, we did get a good deal of reassuring talk from the minister to the effect that there would be no question of loss or default under this agreement; that we could really count on the communist Chinese government to make their payments and that they would be especially anxious to live up to their agreement.

This is what I said on November 29, 1961, to the Saskatchewan farmers union:
There is also the special problem of trade with communist China. X see no reason why-and I said this years ago when it was a far more controversial statement than it is today-we should not trade with communist China in all those commodities which are not on a strategic list upon which we have agreed with our allies. The cold war makes such a list necessary.
While believing this, X think it is hypocriticai for a politician-or indeed for anyone else-to laud the advantages of such trade and then come out categorically against diplomatic recognition of the Peking government "until they have expiated their crimes".
I also believe that it is essential for Canadians to know all the details regarding any trade arrangement with a country like communist China. Such an arrangement on the communist side-and we would be very naive to think otherwise-would only be concluded with Canada, or any other democratic capitalist state, after a cold and careful assessment of communist needs and advantages. Nor would China or any other communist state hesitate to scrap any such arrangement whenever it suited

their purpose to do so. To talk about considerations of honour, their desire to maintain a reputation for honourable dealing, is to be almost childishly ignorant of the nature of communism.
Let us trade, by all means, but let us not deceive ourselves that this kind of business-as long as we have communism and cold war-can be a sound foundation for permanent and expanding trade relations which will be mutually profitable.
With this cautionary qualification regarding trade with communist countries like China, I repeat that we most certainly do need all the expansion of trade we can possibly get, and where we can get it.
Mr. Chairman, I have never at any time said anything which would contradict that point of view. Indeed I repeated that point of view during the election campaign in Wey-burn, Winnipeg and other places.

Well, now, that was one aspect of the minister's speech, and perhaps the most interesting aspect. However, he made another proposal, and he has mentioned it himself. It was certainly surprising to a lot of people, and I will quote it from page 7 of his speech.

RETURN TO PROVINCES OF PUBLIC UTILITIES TAXES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the expediency of introducing legislation in this house that the federal government should return to the provincial treasuries all corporation taxes collected from public utilities within the provinces.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I wish to bring to the attention of the house a situation of gross discrimination prevailing in some provinces of Canada with regard to the taxation of public utilities as well as another similar situation which affects all Canadian consumers, without exception.
I believe that all hon. members in this house sincerely want a great and prosperous Canada which would make progress in good will between all races of which it is composed, whatever the origin and mother tongue of its citizens-a good will which can only be found where there is a spirit of mutual tolerance and mutual understanding. There can be no tolerance and no understanding when discrimination prevails and it would be just empty declamatory talk, just a sequence of high sounding phrases, if we were to hold forth on tolerance and understanding without attacking the roots of what prevents all understanding.
The words "tolerance" and "understanding" have been repeated a hundred times, in every possible form, by every party without exception, and by speakers who were much more eloquent than I am. But have they ever taken concrete steps to uphold those fine theories on matters of principle?
The very basis of national good feeling, is provincial autonomy, an autonomy which it is vain to hope for, if the provinces do not have the necessary financial means to achieve it decently.
I mean in no way to ascribe any intents to anyone, and I shall limit myself to listing a few possible lines of action which would prove that there is a sincere wish to support by deeds words all hon. members keep on repeating.
If certain provinces are discriminated against, it is obvious that those injustices can only cause certain grudges and contribute to the slow but sure disintegration of our country, as it is set up at present. Among those glaring injustices, I shall underline only a few which it would be relatively easy to redress.
Some provinces have nationalized their hydroelectric power a long time ago. Others have done it more recently. As an evident result, of such nationalization, considerable amounts of income taxes paid by private companies to the central government have been taken away from the income of our government. My purpose is not to discuss here the propriety of nationalization by certain provinces of their public utility companies. I only note one irrefutable fact, and it is the following: the Canadian citizens living in certain provinces where public utility companies have not been nationalized contribute more than the citizens of the other provinces to the federal government expenses.
I know that we can claim a certain equalization system which would tend to adjust certain inequalities and injustices, but even after discussing for a long time, on both sides, to consider the good and bad points of that equalization system, there will always remain this brutal fact. According to all established evidence, the citizens of those provinces where public utility companies are operated by private enterprise are penalized on that very count, and it will be useless to laud the merits of private enterprise and to fight for its survival if such injustices are to persist. A province will only have to nationalize certain important sectors of its economy to get away from the severity of the federal taxation, and the whole weight of the federal administration will fall only on the very defenders of private enterprise. Some will refuse to pay so dearly for such convictions.
After having underlined another serious injustice, I will later suggest a means of correcting such a situation.
At the outset of my remarks, I made reference to another field where injustice is general and affects all Canadian consumers, in every province. Of course, a general injustice is a certain form of justice, but a general justice is surely much more desirable and represents a much more sound ideal. It would
1636	HOUSE OF
Corporation Tax Returns to Provinces certainly be less in accordance with distributive justice to inject a disease to everybody, under pretense of equality, than to cure everybody of that same disease.
1 will not go into the details of that other form of injustice. I will only give an example which will apply to all similar cases, that I could multiply indefinitely. In order to remove that injustice, no sacrifice would have to be made either by the federal government or by the provinces, and everybody would be much better off for it.
As has already been mentioned by Mr. W. G. Leonard, professor at the school of commerce of Queen's University, there are two philosophies on the way to administer taxes. According to the first one, taxation, in our democratic system, should be simple, open and readily comprehensible, so as to enable voters to discuss frankly the whole question and to understand the definite relation between government spending and taxation. According to the other philosophy, the art of taxation should be the same as plucking a goose. The object is to get a maximum of feathers with a minimum of shrieks.
The present government, like all previous governments, has chosen to pluck the goose with a minimum of shrieks, and that is how all governments, with the help of the bureaucracy, have evolved a system of disguised taxation, so that the voter cannot discuss fully and with full knowledge the relation between government expenditures and the burden of taxation he bears somewhat unwittingly.
Today, we are living in a country that is over-administered and, therefore over-taxed. Every businessman, every accountant will tell you that a top-heavy administration can lead a sound business to bankruptcy.
What would you think of an industry which would send out a different bill for all the kinds of goods it produces and which would have a different collection service for each product? That is what we are doing by collecting income in several different ways. Is it not the most costly way of achieving a specific aim? Is it not like taking the longest and the most winding road to get somewhere?
It is here, and only here, that we must proceed in an orderly way. Consequently,
I now put forward the following practical proposal:
That the federal government allow all public utilities to deduct from their federal taxes all moneys paid to a provincial government as provincial income tax.

Have not our present difficulties in connection with federal, provincial and municipal tax sharing arisen largely because of the piecemeal approach which has been adopted up to now? We have taken each new problem as it has arisen and tried to deal with it in isolation from the rest of taxation policy. The Canadian tax foundation has been making this point for a number of years and the government has recognized its validity by setting up a royal commission to conduct a thorough study of the tax situation, a study which we hope will lead to a comprehensive overhaul of the whole taxation structure in so far as the federal government is involved and in so far as the federal government can bring about a more equitable distribution of income between the three levels of government.

The provinces have said from time to time that it is improper for the federal government to tax corporations in their provinces which are utilizing this natural resource. As it happens, I believe this problem is mostly significant in the provinces of Quebec and Alberta, and perhaps Newfoundland as well. Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to rise at this time and talk on the motion for fear that my good friend from Quebec East (Mr. Beaule) may accuse me of burying it. I can assure him it is not my intention to do so and can also tell him that those who speak first do as much shovelling as those who speak later. I want to compliment the hon. member on his wit when he said-at least this is what he meant and I agree with his statement-that taxing authorities by and large follow methods to get the most feathers with the least amount of squawk. This is the principle that is followed by taxing authorities in general. I agree with

Corporation Tax Returns to Provinces him on that. There may be some element of truth in what many of the other speakers have said.
There is no question about the fact that the nationalization of resources in certain provinces, especially of hydroelectric, has taken a certain amount of taxation from the federal taxing authority. In so far as that has been done, it has a bearing upon the tax revenues of this country. It also has an indirect bearing on the tax revenues of each province. There are inequities in this area of taxation, as I think everyone would agree, and at some time these particular inequities will need to be studied and solutions found.
The point about which I am concerned in connection with this resolution is the incidence of taxation. The resolution would set up a new principle which would single out public utilities. This is a broad term and I think the hon. member for Quebec East would agree that the term "public utilities" covers far more than he contemplated at the time he worded this resolution. I wonder if when he worded his resolution he did not have in mind simply hydroelectric development? I would say that the term "public utilities" is too broad. I doubt very much if the hon. member would want to give consideration to turning over the taxation of all public utilities to the provincial authority.
Under the system as it is now in most of the provinces, outside of Quebec, most of the taxes are collected by the federal authority. Then, once the revenues are received, they all start to squabble over who is going to get the lion's share. Of course, this is the point at which the resolution starts. The mover of the resolution would like to see all of these revenues which are obtained from public utilities turned over to the provinces. Now, this is a big order. I feel that before we pass a resolution of this kind, the subject would need to be studied, would need to be talked about, would need to be thoroughly considered.
Mind you, sir, what may prevail in Quebec may not fit the situation in Alberta. I am not saying that what the hon. member is advocating is not right for Quebec. All I am saying is that we might prefer something different in Alberta. The hon. member comes from Quebec and I come from Alberta. From a national point of view, when you are entering into a policy of putting the taxation of public utilities into the provincial field you would need to take a look at what you are proposing. I am not attacking the position which the hon. member is taking. All I am saying is that a resolution of this kind deserves the most careful consideration. I think it was well that it was brought before this

house so that we might all take a look at it.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
There is another element contained in this particular resolution which has not been mentioned and I think it should be. I refer to the fact that public utilities are being singled out as the ones on which taxation should be passed to the provinces. There must be some special reason for the Social Credit party to suggest this. When I was thinking about what I should say on this subject, I was wondering whether or not it was because they believed in giving debt free money for the development of public utilities. Since public utilities are not revenue producing, as they say, any taxation according to them could be passed back to the government. I was wondering if there was not some element of this reasoning in the resolution which was not mentioned by the mover. Perhaps he did not have the time to do so, and at some later time he may clarify this for our benefit.
May I call it six o'clock?

Mr. Speaker, I should like, for a moment, to make an appeal to the house leader about the business for tomorrow. I ask him if the government would not reconsider the decision not to continue with the agriculture estimates in view of the fact that decision means that the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) and the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas), who incidentally first raised this problem, are to be prevented from taking part in the debate. In view of the fact that the business the minister has indicated would be taken up tomorrow deals with tax legislation that was

brought before the previous parliament last April, and could have been passed if this parliament had been called in August, I ask the minister if in the interests of freedom of debate and the rights of parliament, the government will not continue with the agriculture estimates tomorrow?

speechtext: What do you know about freedom?
